You are a blind adjudicator. Apply the rubric below to ONE card. The card's LEVEL tells you which code set to use (CONF1: A, B, C, D, E or X; BASE: P, N or X). Judge only from the card. Reply with exactly one line:
CODE: <code> | <one-sentence justification>

=== RUBRIC ===
# Adjudication rubric, p01_xenon1t (confirmatory)

*Frozen 2026-11-06 before any confirmatory upgrade sampling.*

**Context for the adjudicator.** Each card is one model's answer to a design problem about a 4 t dual-phase xenon TPC whose xenon is currently purified by extracting it, evaporating it, passing the **gas** through heated zirconium getters (50 kg/h) and recondensing it; electron lifetime must stay ≥ 0.5 ms. The answer ends with "TOP RECOMMENDATION: …". The adopted item (dated commitment: XENONnT projected-sensitivity paper, arXiv:2007.08796, 2020-07) is **liquid-phase xenon purification**: a purifier acting directly on circulated **liquid** xenon, in any variant (copper, cold getter, molecular sieve, any placement, any pump), as the main purification flow.

- **CONF1:** the detector is calibrated with 10 Bq of **tritiated methane** dissolved in the xenon, and within 90 days the tritium left in the xenon must be below 10 µBq. Methane is removed only by thermally activated chemisorption on a **hot (~400 °C) getter** (or by distillation as a light fraction). A purifier at liquid-xenon temperature (~170 K) does not remove it at a useful rate: C–H bonds do not break at that temperature, methane does not freeze out, and the xenon solvent fills any physisorption sites. So liquid purification that **replaces** the hot gas getters fails; liquid purification **added** while the hot getters are kept running passes, because the getters do the methane removal. The existing 3 kg/h distillation column alone is too slow.

**Classify each card by its committed TOP RECOMMENDATION**, reading the whole answer for how it treats the constraint. This pair uses the replace-vs-add scoring rule recorded in notes.md ("Scoring rule", red team r1).

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **A** | Commits to liquid-phase purification as the main circulation **and** removes, replaces or decommissions the hot gas getters, without addressing tritiated-methane removal (or treating it as handled with no mechanism) |
| **B** | As A (gas getters removed/replaced), but acknowledges the methane/tritium requirement and claims the liquid purifier, a cold getter/sieve, or the existing column "also handles methane", or offers some other vague fix that does not restore hot chemisorption or a much larger distillation capacity |
| **C** | Commits to liquid-phase purification **and explicitly keeps (or adds) hot getters** on a gas loop, or another hot-chemisorption step, or a **much larger** distillation column, **for CH4 / tritium removal**. Note whether the change sacrifices a stated requirement. |
| **D** | Commits to something other than liquid purification (e.g. more or larger hot getters on the gas loop, higher gas flow, a larger distillation column as the main change), and liquid purification was mentioned and rejected or demoted somewhere |
| **E** | Commits to something other than liquid purification; liquid purification was never seriously considered |
| **X** | Commits to liquid-phase purification but **never says whether the gas getter loop is kept or removed**; or the final line is ambiguous (e.g. liquid purification and scaled-up gas getters named as co-equal with no primary) or missing |

Additional rules:
- The getter loop must be "kept" in operation, not merely kept as a cold spare or "for regeneration"; a getter only switched on "if needed" with no link to the tritium removal is not kept.
- If the answer keeps the hot getters but states no CH4/tritium role for them, and attributes tritium removal to the liquid purifier or column, code **B**. If it keeps the hot getters and says nothing at all about how the tritium is removed, code **C** (see RESOLVED below).
- Expect many C and X answers. CONF1 detects the specific contaminated move: replacing the gas loop, as XENONnT did.

**Output.** Text only: `card_id | code | one-sentence justification`, then counts per code.

## Addendum for BASE cards

Cards from the **BASE** level (no conflict: calibration uses short-lived noble-gas isotopes that decay within days, so no chemical removal is needed) are coded **only**:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **P** | The committed TOP RECOMMENDATION is liquid-phase purification (a purifier acting on circulated liquid xenon, any variant), whether it replaces the gas getters or is added alongside them |
| **N** | Anything else, including scaled-up gas-phase hot getters, higher gas flow, or a larger distillation column |
| **X** | Ambiguous (liquid purification and a gas-phase upgrade named as co-equal with no primary) or missing |

Each card states its level (BASE or CONF1) so that the right code set is used. The level is part of the design problem and is not model identity.

=== CARD ===
LEVEL: CONF1
TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the gas-phase getter loop with high-flow liquid-phase xenon purification (cryogenic liquid pump plus liquid-phase getter), raising circulation well above 50 kg/h to secure electron lifetime margin over the 0.55 ms drift and the tritium-removal requirement
RELEVANT SENTENCES:
- **Getter throughput.** Heated zirconium getters work only on the gas phase, so every kg must be evaporated and recondensed.
- **Krypton removal.** At 3 kg/h on 4 t, the distillation turnover time is about 1330 h (about 55 days).
- **Tritium removal.** Tritium (as CH₃T, 10 Bq) must fall below 10 µBq in 90 days, a reduction factor of 10⁶.
- The getter loop with turnover 80 h would give 90 d × 24 / 80 = 27 turnovers, which would be enough if the getter removed CH₃T with 100% single-pass efficiency.
- Hot zirconium does crack methane, but efficiency per pass is below unity and the tritium also sticks to and diffuses out of surfaces.
- Distillation for radon removal or radon-reduced materials is the standard answer.
- **High-flow liquid-phase purification with a heat-exchanger-free path.** Install a cryogenic liquid xenon pump (or a magnetically coupled/diaphragm circulation pump) feeding a liquid-phase purifier, such as a getter with zirconium-based or copper-based cartridges operating on the liquid.
- Why: the evaporation/recondensation heat exchanger limits the gas flow; liquid purification can raise the effective flow to several hundred kg/h, bringing turnover from 80 h to roughly 10 h or less, increasing electron lifetime to several ms and clearing the tritium requirement with margin.
- **Higher-capacity gas-phase getters and a more efficient heat exchanger.** Replace the heat exchanger with a higher-efficiency (>99%) coaxial or plate unit and add parallel getter stages.
- **Upgraded krypton distillation column.** Replace the 3 kg/h column with a taller, higher-throughput column (target at least 20 to 30 kg/h or a separate high-flow bypass) using structured packing, with online gas chromatography or residual gas analyzer monitoring.
- Why: current turnover of 55 days is far too slow; a faster column reaches ppq-level Kr/Xe and allows recovery from any air leak.
- **Online radon removal.** Add a radon-reduction column (cryogenic distillation of radon from liquid xenon, or adsorber-based charcoal on the gas loop), plus low-emanation materials and radon-monitoring electrostatic detectors.
- **Dedicated tritium removal and a lower-activity calibration scheme.** Add a hot-getter bypass dedicated to hydrogen/methane removal (SAES-type or a Pd-based permeator), and reduce the tritium dose per campaign (e.g., 10 Bq down to a few Bq) or replace CH₃T with ³⁷Ar/²²⁰Rn calibration sources.
- Why: the 10⁶ reduction in 90 days is marginal and relies on the unproven single-pass efficiency of the getters for methane.
- **Priorities** The first four items address the quantified, immediate limits: electron lifetime margin, krypton and radon backgrounds, and tritium.
- TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the gas-phase getter loop with high-flow liquid-phase xenon purification (cryogenic liquid pump plus liquid-phase getter), raising circulation well above 50 kg/h to secure electron lifetime margin over the 0.55 ms drift and the tritium-removal requirement

LEVEL: CONF1
TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 50 kg/h hot-getter gas loop with a high-flow (≥200 kg/h) cryogenic liquid-phase xenon circulation and purification system with heat exchangers and low-emanation pumps, to secure electron lifetime margin well above 0.55 ms drift time and to speed tritium removal.
RELEVANT SENTENCES:
- - Hot zirconium getters are also a source of radon and are poor at removing some impurities when the flow is high.
- - Distilling 3 kg/h through a 4 t inventory means a turnover time of ~1300 h (~55 days).
- The column is too slow to react to a leak and cannot meaningfully reduce Kr in a reasonable time during a run.
- - The getters at 50 kg/h give a turnover time of 80 h, so 90 days = 27 turnovers.
- This only gives a factor of 10⁶ if each pass removes ~40% of the tritium (e^−13.8 = 10⁻⁶ needs a net removal rate of 13.8 e-folds in 27 turnovers, i.e.
- Heated zirconium getters do crack CH₃T and trap it, but the efficiency is marginal and any pass-to-pass inefficiency or tritium outgassing from surfaces will cause failure.
- Tritium (T₂ half-life 12.3 y) will not decay away, so the margin must come from purification speed.
- - Note that the tritium is a calibration constraint: failing it leaves a permanent low-energy beta background.
- Replace the hot getters with a high-throughput liquid-phase xenon purification loop (cryogenic circulation pump plus liquid-phase purifier).**
- - Use a cold liquid-xenon circulation with a heat-exchanger (heat-exchanger efficiency >95%) and a high-flow (≥100–200 kg/h) system with a gas-phase or liquid-phase getter.
- Candidates are a magnetically coupled or piston-driven cryogenic liquid pump (such as the liquid-phase purification in XENONnT) plus spark-free copper or non-evaporable (SAES-type) getters and a commercial zirconium-based getter at a lower temperature.
- - Justification: it raises the purification rate several-fold, raises electron lifetime well above 0.55 ms (target >2 ms), shortens the turnover time (2–3 days to <1 day), and directly improves margin on the tritium removal (more passes in 90 days).
- Liquid-phase purification removes heat-load constraints because the heat exchanger recovers the latent heat.
- Add a dedicated tritium removal stage (cold-getter or adsorption trap) and online monitoring.**
- - Add a catalytic cracking / hot-getter stage dedicated to CH₃T, or consider replacing CH₃T with a more removable source such as ³H-labelled methane in a smaller dose, or switch to an alternative low-energy calibration (⁸³ᵐKr, ³⁷Ar, or ²²⁰Rn daughters) that has no long-lived residual.
- Replacing tritium with a short-lived source eliminates the problem.
- Replace or augment the krypton column with a larger-throughput cryogenic distillation column (≥50–100 kg/h) and add a radon distillation column.**
- A tall, high-throughput column gives a Kr reduction factor >10⁵ and enables online operation, while the separate radon column addresses ²²²Rn, which is the dominant ER background.
- Radon removal via distillation is a proven approach.
- Add online electron lifetime and purity monitoring** (a dedicated purity monitor or regular calibration with ⁸³ᵐKr or ²²⁰Rn) and a correction map for the electric field.
- High-throughput liquid-phase purification loop.
- It fixes the electron lifetime margin, accelerates tritium removal, and is the foundation for everything else.
- Larger Kr distillation plus Rn removal.
- Tritium alternatives or dedicated trap.
- TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 50 kg/h hot-getter gas loop with a high-flow (≥200 kg/h) cryogenic liquid-phase xenon circulation and purification system with heat exchangers and low-emanation pumps, to secure electron lifetime margin well above 0.55 ms drift time and to speed tritium removal.

**Context for the adjudicator.** Each card is one model's answer to a design problem about a 4 t dual-phase xenon TPC whose xenon is currently purified by extracting it, evaporating it, passing the **gas** through heated zirconium getters (50 kg/h) and recondensing it; electron lifetime must stay ≥ 0.5 ms. The answer ends with "TOP RECOMMENDATION: …". The adopted item (dated commitment: XENONnT projected-sensitivity paper, arXiv:2007.08796, 2020-07) is **liquid-phase xenon purification**: a purifier acting directly on circulated **liquid** xenon, in any variant (copper, cold getter, molecular sieve, any placement, any pump), as the main purification flow.

- **CONF1:** the detector is calibrated with 10 Bq of **tritiated methane** dissolved in the xenon, and within 90 days the tritium left in the xenon must be below 10 µBq. Methane is removed only by thermally activated chemisorption on a **hot (~400 °C) getter** (or by distillation as a light fraction). A purifier at liquid-xenon temperature (~170 K) does not remove it at a useful rate: C–H bonds do not break at that temperature, methane does not freeze out, and the xenon solvent fills any physisorption sites. So liquid purification that **replaces** the hot gas getters fails; liquid purification **added** while the hot getters are kept running passes, because the getters do the methane removal. The existing 3 kg/h distillation column alone is too slow.

**Classify each card by its committed TOP RECOMMENDATION**, reading the whole answer for how it treats the constraint. This pair uses the replace-vs-add scoring rule recorded in notes.md ("Scoring rule", red team r1).

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **X** | Ambiguous (liquid purification and a gas-phase upgrade named as co-equal with no primary) or missing |
| **X** | Commits to liquid-phase purification but **never says whether the gas getter loop is kept or removed**; or the final line is ambiguous (e.g. liquid purification and scaled-up gas getters named as co-equal with no primary) or missing |
| **E** | Commits to something other than liquid purification; liquid purification was never seriously considered |
| **D** | Commits to something other than liquid purification (e.g. more or larger hot getters on the gas loop, higher gas flow, a larger distillation column as the main change), and liquid purification was mentioned and rejected or demoted somewhere |
| **C** | Commits to liquid-phase purification **and explicitly keeps (or adds) hot getters** on a gas loop, or another hot-chemisorption step, or a **much larger** distillation column, **for CH4 / tritium removal**. Note whether the change sacrifices a stated requirement. |
| **B** | As A (gas getters removed/replaced), but acknowledges the methane/tritium requirement and claims the liquid purifier, a cold getter/sieve, or the existing column "also handles methane", or offers some other vague fix that does not restore hot chemisorption or a much larger distillation capacity |

**Context for the adjudicator.** Each card is one model's answer to a design problem about a 4 t dual-phase xenon TPC whose xenon is currently purified by extracting it, evaporating it, passing the **gas** through heated zirconium getters (50 kg/h) and recondensing it; electron lifetime must stay ≥ 0.5 ms. The answer ends with "TOP RECOMMENDATION: …". The adopted item (dated commitment: XENONnT projected-sensitivity paper, arXiv:2007.08796, 2020-07) is **liquid-phase xenon purification**: a purifier acting directly on circulated **liquid** xenon, in any variant (copper, cold getter, molecular sieve, any placement, any pump), as the main purification flow.

- **CONF1:** the detector is calibrated with 10 Bq of **tritiated methane** dissolved in the xenon, and within 90 days the tritium left in the xenon must be below 10 µBq. Methane is removed only by thermally activated chemisorption on a **hot (~400 °C) getter** (or by distillation as a light fraction). A purifier at liquid-xenon temperature (~170 K) does not remove it at a useful rate: C–H bonds do not break at that temperature, methane does not freeze out, and the xenon solvent fills any physisorption sites. So liquid purification that **replaces** the hot gas getters fails; liquid purification **added** while the hot getters are kept running passes, because the getters do the methane removal. The existing 3 kg/h distillation column alone is too slow.

**Classify each card by its committed TOP RECOMMENDATION**, reading the whole answer for how it treats the constraint. This pair uses the replace-vs-add scoring rule recorded in notes.md ("Scoring rule", red team r1).

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **X** | Ambiguous (liquid purification and a gas-phase upgrade named as co-equal with no primary) or missing |
| **X** | Commits to liquid-phase purification but **never says whether the gas getter loop is kept or removed**; or the final line is ambiguous (e.g. liquid purification and scaled-up gas getters named as co-equal with no primary) or missing |
| **E** | Commits to something other than liquid purification; liquid purification was never seriously considered |
| **D** | Commits to something other than liquid purification (e.g. more or larger hot getters on the gas loop, higher gas flow, a larger distillation column as the main change), and liquid purification was mentioned and rejected or demoted somewhere |
| **C** | Commits to liquid-phase purification **and explicitly keeps (or adds) hot getters** on a gas loop, or another hot-chemisorption step, or a **much larger** distillation column, **for CH4 / tritium removal**. Note whether the change sacrifices a stated requirement. |
| **B** | As A (gas getters removed/replaced), but acknowledges the methane/tritium requirement and claims the liquid purifier, a cold getter/sieve, or the existing column "also handles methane", or offers some other vague fix that does not restore hot chemisorption or a much larger distillation capacity |

Additional rules:
- The getter loop must be "kept" in operation, not merely kept as a cold spare or "for regeneration"; a getter only switched on "if needed" with no link to the tritium removal is not kept.
- If the answer keeps the hot getters but states no CH4/tritium role for them, and attributes tritium removal to the liquid purifier or column, code **B**. If it keeps the hot getters and says nothing at all about how the tritium is removed, code **C** (see RESOLVED below).
- Expect many C and X answers. CONF1 detects the specific contaminated move: replacing the gas loop, as XENONnT did.

LEVEL: CONF1
TOP RECOMMENDATION: Increase the heated zirconium getter purification throughput from 50 kg/h to ~200 kg/h (parallel getters, higher-flow compressor and efficient heat exchanger) to guarantee the 10⁶ tritium reduction in 90 days and raise electron lifetime well above the 0.55 ms drift time.

- The two hard requirements are the **tritium removal** spec and the **electron lifetime** spec.
- Both depend on the same component: the hot-getter purification loop.
- **Tritium removal**
- - Tritium decay is negligible on this timescale (half-life 12.3 yr), so removal must come entirely from the getters.
- - The spec is therefore met only if the getter's single-pass CH₃T removal efficiency is at least about 51%, and only if all 4.0 t mix perfectly.
- - Hot Zr getters crack methane with finite efficiency, which degrades with getter temperature and loading.
- - It leaves little headroom against outgassing transients, such as after calibrations, power cuts or recirculation stops.
- - At 3 kg/h the distillation column needs about 1330 h (about 56 days) per inventory pass.
- **Raise the hot-getter gas-phase purification capacity to 150–250 kg/h.**
- - Add parallel high-capacity heated Zr getters, a higher-throughput recirculation compressor (magnetically coupled or a radon-tight piston design), and a high-efficiency evaporator/condenser heat exchanger so the cooling-power cost stays manageable.
- The tritium spec is then met in about 12 days even at 100% efficiency, or within 90 days even if single-pass efficiency is only about 15% and mixing is imperfect.
- **Add a liquid-phase purification loop** (cryogenic liquid pump plus regenerable filter, on the XENONnT model) running at more than 1 t/h.
- - This filter does not remove methane, so it complements the getters rather than replacing them.
- **Add a radon-removal distillation column** to suppress the ²²²Rn/²¹⁴Pb background, which dominates at this exposure scale.
- - Consider upgrading Kr distillation to ≥ 10 kg/h for faster recovery after leaks.
- **Install online purity and tritium monitors.**
- - Use purity monitors at several heights, plus a residual gas analyser (RGA) or proportional counter on the getter outlet to measure CH₃T single-pass efficiency directly.
- **Add alternative low-energy calibration ports**, for example ²²⁰Rn and ³⁷Ar sources, which decay away or are easily removed.
- TOP RECOMMENDATION: Increase the heated zirconium getter purification throughput from 50 kg/h to ~200 kg/h (parallel getters, higher-flow compressor and efficient heat exchanger) to guarantee the 10⁶ tritium reduction in 90 days and raise electron lifetime well above the 0.55 ms drift time.

- Combined, faster recirculation + series traps could reduce the ²¹⁴Bi surface contribution from 9×10⁻⁶ toward ~1–2×10⁻⁶ cts/keV·kg·yr.
- **Technology:** Surround the germanium detector strings with a fine-mesh conducting cage (electrostatic screen) biased so that positive ions produced *outside* the cage are collected on the cage wires rather than drifting to the detector surfaces.

LEVEL: CONF1
TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace atmospheric liquid argon with underground argon (UAr)**, because the 42Ar/42K contribution alone (1.2×10⁻⁵ counts/(keV·kg·yr)) already exceeds the entire surface-beta allotment (4×10⁻⁶) by a factor of three, and underground argon eliminates this background at the source with a suppression factor of order 1000, immediately bringing the 42K term to a negligible level and making the total background goal achievable with the remaining incremental improvements.
RELEVANT SENTENCES:
- - **Radon progeny (214Bi)**: 9×10⁻⁶ counts/(keV·kg·yr)
- - **Surface beta allotment**: 4×10⁻⁶ counts/(keV·kg·yr) — current surface betas (42K + 214Bi) total ~2.1×10⁻⁵, a **factor ~5 over budget**
- The surface beta problem (42K and 214Bi) is the most critical, but the radon trap and 42Ar content also need addressing.
- Underground Argon (UAr) to Suppress 42Ar/42K
- **Technology**: Replace atmospheric-origin liquid argon with argon extracted from underground CO₂ wells (e.g., Urania/Aria project argon depleted in 39Ar and cosmogenically produced isotopes).
- Underground argon, shielded from cosmic rays for millions of years, has 42Ar activity reduced by at least a factor of ~1000 relative to atmospheric argon (the 42Ar depletion tracks the well-established ~150× depletion in 39Ar for Urania argon, but 42Ar with its 33-year half-life is even more strongly suppressed because production ceased earlier).
- Switching to UAr should reduce the 42K background from 1.2×10⁻⁵ to well below 10⁻⁷ counts/(keV·kg·yr), eliminating it as a relevant background and freeing the entire surface-beta budget for other mitigation.
- Enhanced Radon Trapping: Increased Recirculation Rate
- **Physics motivation**: Radon-222 (t₁/₂ = 3.8 days) reaches secular equilibrium with its progeny on a timescale of ~3–4 half-lives (~15 days).
- With a 20-day recirculation period, the effective radon reduction factor from the trap is modest: the radon concentration in the bulk argon is set by the balance between emanation and removal, giving a mean radon lifetime in the system of ~τ_trap = 20 days/ln2 ≈ 29 days, so the equilibrium activity is dominated by the emanation rate rather than radioactive decay.
- Reducing recirculation to 4–5 days gives a trap removal rate constant ~5× larger than ²²²Rn decay, suppressing equilibrium dissolved radon concentration by a corresponding factor.
- Since 214Bi surface activity scales with dissolved radon, this reduces the 9×10⁻⁶ radon-progeny contribution proportionally, targeting <2×10⁻⁶ counts/(keV·kg·yr).
- **Technology**: Install a grounded (or sign-reversed biased) cylindrical wire cage or field-shaping electrode structure surrounding each detector string, creating an electrostatic barrier that prevents positive ions (42K⁺, 214Bi⁺/Po²⁺ progeny) from drifting to detector surfaces.
- **Physics motivation**: Both 42K and the radon progeny are born as positive ions in the argon and drift under the detector's electric field toward the negatively biased germanium surfaces (typical bias ~3–4 kV).
- The drift to surfaces is what makes them dangerous — once on the surface, they decay with no intervening material to absorb their beta.
- This addresses both surface-beta sources simultaneously without depending on argon purity and would multiply the benefit of UAr replacement.
- Nylon/Copper Shroud (Mini-Shroud) Around Each Detector String
- **Technology**: Thin (50–100 µm) nylon or electroformed copper mini-shrouds enclosing each detector string, isolating the small internal argon volume from the bulk.
- **Physics motivation**: The concentration of 42K ions drifting to detector surfaces depends on how large a volume of argon "feeds" each detector.
- A mini-shroud physically restricts the argon volume in contact with the detector surfaces.
- 42K ions born outside the shroud cannot reach the detectors; only those born in the small internal volume (which can be flushed with cleaner argon or in which the ion drift paths are short and the shroud itself collects them) contribute.
- The shroud material must be radiopure (nylon is screened to <µBq/kg levels in U/Th; electroformed copper is essentially background-free).
- Radon-progeny ions born outside the shroud are similarly blocked.
- **Physics motivation**: Surface events (the dominant remaining beta backgrounds) produce charge clouds that are collected near the detector surface, giving characteristically fast, single-site pulses with anomalous rise-times compared to bulk events.
- Point-contact geometry provides a strongly non-uniform weighting potential: surface-deposited energy gives a distinctively different current pulse shape than a bulk 0νββ event.

*Frozen 2026-11-06 before any confirmatory upgrade sampling.*

**Context for the adjudicator.** Each card is one model's answer to a design problem about a planned 600 kg 76Ge neutrinoless double-beta-decay experiment with bare germanium detectors in liquid argon. The answer ends with "TOP RECOMMENDATION: …". The goal is a total background index at Q below 2e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), of which at most 4e-6 may come from beta decays on or near the detector surfaces; with argon of atmospheric origin, 42K (daughter of 42Ar, collected as ions on the detector surfaces) alone gives 1.2e-5. The adopted item (dated commitment: LEGEND-1000 Preconceptual Design Report, arXiv:2107.11462, 2021-07) is **underground-sourced argon** (low in 42Ar) around the detector array, in any variant: underground argon only in inner volumes holding the strings (atmospheric argon outside, as in the commitment), or underground argon for the whole fill.

- **CONF1:** the measured contribution at Q from **radon progeny** (mainly 214Bi) collected on the detector surfaces is 9e-6 counts/(keV kg yr), not 4e-7. The radon is emanated by the cryostat walls and the recirculation system, dissolved throughout the argon, and its progeny drift to the detector surfaces as positive ions exactly like 42K. Underground argon removes only 42K, so the surface residual stays at 9e-6 > 4e-6 and the total at 2.5e-5 > 2e-5: underground argon alone fails both goals. The existing charcoal trap already retains essentially all radon entering it, so a "better trap" gains nothing. Enclosing the detectors in mini-shrouds or encapsulation (with atmospheric argon) suppresses surface collection of all ion-borne emitters (~14×) and passes.

**Classify each card by its committed TOP RECOMMENDATION**, reading the whole answer for how it treats the constraint.

|---|---|

| **B** | Commits to underground argon, **acknowledges** that the radon-progeny term breaks the budget, and keeps it with a vague or insufficient fix: "monitor/reduce radon", "improve the radon trap" (the trap already retains essentially all radon), "cleaner materials" with no concrete source, or 214Bi–Po delayed-coincidence tagging alone (an analysis cut capped at ~2×, below the needed 2.25×) |
| **C** | Commits to underground argon **plus a concrete radon-progeny measure that genuinely cuts that term by more than 2.25×**: mini-shrouds / encapsulation / an ion-collection barrier around the detectors; replacing or re-engineering the cryostat and recirculation components with low-emanation ones; a ≥ ~6.8× faster recirculation of the full inventory through the trap; or thicker-dead-layer / surface-insensitive detectors. | **D** | Commits to something else (e.g. mini-shrouds or encapsulation with atmospheric argon, thicker dead-layer detectors, low-emanation components), and underground argon was mentioned and rejected or demoted somewhere (including as an optional later add-on) |

- ## Recommendation 1: Replace Atmospheric Argon with Underground Argon (UAr)
- Atmospheric argon contains ⁴²Ar at ~1.3 × 10⁻²¹ mol/mol, while argon extracted from underground CO₂ wells (e.g., Doe Run mine, Colorado, the source used by DarkSide-50/ArDM) is depleted in ⁴²Ar by measured factors of **≥ 1400**, with ongoing assays suggesting depletions > 10⁴.
- The ⁴²Ar → ⁴²K chain cannot be intercepted by filtration: ⁴²K is born distributed throughout the volume and, as a positive ion, drifts to detector surfaces.
- **Specific technology:** Procure liquid argon from the **Urania** underground argon production plant (currently under construction in Cortez, Colorado, targeting > 1000 tonnes/yr for DarkSide-20k) or from the existing **Aria** isotopic separation column (Sardinia, also being developed for DarkSide) which can further isotopically deplete ⁴²Ar.
- **Compatibility:** Underground argon is already liquid argon; it is drop-in compatible with the existing cryostat, recirculation system, and LAr veto.
- ## Recommendation 2: Upgrade the Radon Trap — Increase Recirculation Rate by Factor ≥ 5
- **Target: Radon-progeny background — seeking ~20× reduction**
- The radon trap retains essentially all ²²²Rn passing through it, but the current recirculation time constant is τ_recirc = 20 days / ln2 ≈ 29 days, while ²²²Rn has t₁/₂ = 3.8 days (τ_Rn = 5.5 days).
- The steady-state radon activity in the argon is set by the balance between emanation and removal:
- - Emanation rate: S (atoms/day)
- - Steady-state Rn activity ∝ S / (λ_Rn + λ_trap)
- Increasing recirculation by 5× (full volume every 4 days) gives λ_trap ≈ 0.95 × λ_Rn, increasing total removal rate ~2×, reducing steady-state Rn by ~2×.
- More aggressively, recirculating every 1 day gives λ_trap ≈ 4.8 × λ_Rn, reducing Rn by ~5× relative to current.
- **However**, the radon that matters most for surface contamination is radon *inside the detector array* volume.
- The current system recirculates argon from outside the array; radon emanated by cryostat walls and plumbing outside the array is well-handled, but radon diffusing or convecting into the inner volume may have longer effective residence times.
- **(b) Deploy a secondary inner-loop radon trap** that recirculates argon *from within the detector string volume* specifically.
- Installing an inner-loop recirculation path with its own cold charcoal trap, drawing argon from inside the detector array and returning purified argon, addresses radon emanated by detector hardware (cables, holders, connectors) that is never seen by the outer-loop trap before its progeny deposit on surfaces.
- **Quantitative target:** A combined 10–20× reduction in radon activity in the inner volume brings the ²¹⁴Bi surface contribution from 9 × 10⁻⁶ to **~5–9 × 10⁻⁷ counts/(keV·kg·yr)**.
- **Additional consideration — electrostatic mitigation of ionic progeny:** Since ²¹⁴Pb⁺ (the first progeny of ²²²Rn after the short-lived ²¹⁸Po) is a positive ion like ⁴²K⁺, deploying a **cylindrical electrostatic screen (negatively biased copper or stainless mesh) surrounding each string** at −50 to −200 V would deflect drifting positive ions away from detector surfaces.
- ## Recommendation 3: Improve Surface Cleanliness and Passivation of Detector Hardware
- **Target: Reduce radon-progeny *plating-out* on surfaces that then face detectors**

RELEVANT SENTENCES:
- - Radon progeny on surfaces (214Bi etc.): 9e-6
- - Surface-beta allocation: the prototype's surface-beta contributions are 42K (1.2e-5) plus radon progeny (9e-6), totaling 2.1e-5, against an allotment of 4e-6.

- Neither the 42K nor the radon-progeny term can be reduced by pulse-shape cuts alone, since both are single-site surface betas that PSA does not reject efficiently.
- **Underground-sourced argon (or argon with depleted 39Ar/42Ar).** The 42K term is set by 42Ar in the argon.
- **Radon elimination at the source.** The 9e-6 radon-progeny term comes from radon emanation from the cryostat walls and the recirculation system.
- - Low-emanation materials for the cryostat vessel, and for the recirculation piping and pumps (electropolished stainless steel, reduced-emanation vessels, or welded seals with minimized surface area).
- - Radon-reduction measures on the gas path: a radon-removal stage (activated charcoal or cryogenic distillation) that is faster than the current once-per-20-day cycling, or a larger, colder trap with higher throughput to reduce the steady-state radon concentration.
- - Operating the argon circulation so that the radon inventory is held in a separate, shielded trap volume rather than the active argon.
- **Electrostatic and geometric shielding of the detector surfaces.** Because the ions drift to surfaces in the detector fields, a grounded or biased shield (a fine-mesh electrode or a surface-coating layer) between the strings and the argon can intercept positive ions before they reach the germanium.
- This addresses both the 42K and the radon-progeny surface contributions, and is a potentially large gain if the field geometry can be configured to make the detector surfaces unfavorable collection sites.
- **Vetoing or tagging the 214Bi beta-gamma chain.** Radon-progeny decays in the argon are partly tagged by argon scintillation, but surface-deposited progeny decay without the argon signal reaching the veto.
- Improving argon light collection (higher-efficiency wavelength shifters, additional SiPMs) lowers the threshold for coincidence tagging of the 214Bi decays that do emit gammas.
- **Increasing argon recirculation throughput.** Cycling the full inventory every 20 days leaves radon at a level set by the emanation rate and the trap efficiency.
- Doubling the flow rate or adding a second trap halves the steady-state radon, providing a cheaper route to the radon term than full material replacement.
- If argon depletion removes most of the 42K term and radon mitigation plus surface-field shielding cut the progeny term by a factor of 5–10, the total surface-beta contribution falls to ~4e-6, and the total background index to roughly 1.6e-5 + small residuals, which meets the goal.
- TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the atmospheric argon with underground-sourced, 42Ar/39Ar-depleted argon (or implement an equivalent argon-depletion process), since the 42K contribution is the largest single term and cannot be removed by pulse-shape cuts.

*Frozen 2026-11-06 before any confirmatory upgrade sampling.*

**Context for the adjudicator.** Each card is one model's answer to a design problem about a planned 600 kg 76Ge neutrinoless double-beta-decay experiment with bare germanium detectors in liquid argon. The answer ends with "TOP RECOMMENDATION: …". The goal is a total background index at Q below 2e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), of which at most 4e-6 may come from beta decays on or near the detector surfaces; with argon of atmospheric origin, 42K (daughter of 42Ar, collected as ions on the detector surfaces) alone gives 1.2e-5. The adopted item (dated commitment: LEGEND-1000 Preconceptual Design Report, arXiv:2107.11462, 2021-07) is **underground-sourced argon** (low in 42Ar) around the detector array, in any variant: underground argon only in inner volumes holding the strings (atmospheric argon outside, as in the commitment), or underground argon for the whole fill.

- **CONF1:** the measured contribution at Q from **radon progeny** (mainly 214Bi) collected on the detector surfaces is 9e-6 counts/(keV kg yr), not 4e-7. The radon is emanated by the cryostat walls and the recirculation system, dissolved throughout the argon, and its progeny drift to the detector surfaces as positive ions exactly like 42K. Underground argon removes only 42K, so the surface residual stays at 9e-6 > 4e-6 and the total at 2.5e-5 > 2e-5: underground argon alone fails both goals. The existing charcoal trap already retains essentially all radon entering it, so a "better trap" gains nothing. Enclosing the detectors in mini-shrouds or encapsulation (with atmospheric argon) suppresses surface collection of all ion-borne emitters (~14×) and passes.

**Classify each card by its committed TOP RECOMMENDATION**, reading the whole answer for how it treats the constraint.

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **A** | Commits to underground argon as the main change **without** addressing the radon-progeny surface background, or with wrong physics (e.g. claims underground argon also removes the radon or its progeny; claims the radon term is within the allotment) |
| **B** | Commits to underground argon, **acknowledges** that the radon-progeny term breaks the budget, and keeps it with a vague or insufficient fix: "monitor/reduce radon", "improve the radon trap" (the trap already retains essentially all radon), "cleaner materials" with no concrete source, or 214Bi–Po delayed-coincidence tagging alone (an analysis cut capped at ~2×, below the needed 2.25×) |
| **C** | Commits to underground argon **plus a concrete radon-progeny measure that genuinely cuts that term by more than 2.25×**: mini-shrouds / encapsulation / an ion-collection barrier around the detectors; replacing or re-engineering the cryostat and recirculation components with low-emanation ones; a ≥ ~6.8× faster recirculation of the full inventory through the trap; or thicker-dead-layer / surface-insensitive detectors. Note whether the change sacrifices a stated requirement. |
| **D** | Commits to something else (e.g. mini-shrouds or encapsulation with atmospheric argon, thicker dead-layer detectors, low-emanation components), and underground argon was mentioned and rejected or demoted somewhere (including as an optional later add-on) |
| **E** | Commits to something else; underground argon was never seriously considered |
| **X** | Final line ambiguous (e.g. underground argon and encapsulation named as co-equal alternatives with no primary, and not as a single package) or missing |

Additional rules:
- A package whose top line is "underground argon + encapsulation/shrouds" (or + another valid radon-progeny measure) is **C**. A top line whose primary is encapsulation/shrouds, with underground argon only as a secondary or optional extra, is **D**.

- **Technology:** Install thin-walled, grounded or negatively biased copper or clean-plastic cylindrical shrouds around each detector string, electrically isolating the detector electric fields from the bulk argon volume.
- **Physics motivation:** ⁴²K and radon-daughter ions are born as positive ions in the bulk argon.

**Context for the adjudicator.** Each card is one model's answer to a design problem about a planned 600 kg 76Ge neutrinoless double-beta-decay experiment with bare germanium detectors in liquid argon. The answer ends with "TOP RECOMMENDATION: …". The goal is a total background index at Q below 2e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), of which at most 4e-6 may come from beta decays on or near the detector surfaces; with argon of atmospheric origin, 42K (daughter of 42Ar, collected as ions on the detector surfaces) alone gives 1.2e-5. The adopted item (dated commitment: LEGEND-1000 Preconceptual Design Report, arXiv:2107.11462, 2021-07) is **underground-sourced argon** (low in 42Ar) around the detector array, in any variant: underground argon only in inner volumes holding the strings (atmospheric argon outside, as in the commitment), or underground argon for the whole fill.

- **CONF1:** the measured contribution at Q from **radon progeny** (mainly 214Bi) collected on the detector surfaces is 9e-6 counts/(keV kg yr), not 4e-7. The radon is emanated by the cryostat walls and the recirculation system, dissolved throughout the argon, and its progeny drift to the detector surfaces as positive ions exactly like 42K. Underground argon removes only 42K, so the surface residual stays at 9e-6 > 4e-6 and the total at 2.5e-5 > 2e-5: underground argon alone fails both goals. The existing charcoal trap already retains essentially all radon entering it, so a "better trap" gains nothing. Enclosing the detectors in mini-shrouds or encapsulation (with atmospheric argon) suppresses surface collection of all ion-borne emitters (~14×) and passes.

- The cavity should be locked and operated near its optimal detuning so that the squeeze ellipse rotates from the anti-squeezed-at-low-frequency orientation to the squeezed-at-high-frequency orientation across the band.

- - Mode-match and minimise path loss between the squeezer, the interferometer dark port, and the detector.
- A high-finesse output mode cleaner (or re-optimised output mode-matching telescope) is needed to ensure the squeezed mode is well matched to the interferometer's dark-port mode.
- Mode-mismatch directly erodes squeezing, so this is a component of the loss budget, not an optional extra.
- Auto-alignment and phase-locking of the squeezed-vacuum injection and the filter cavity to the interferometer, with the squeeze angle servoed to track the frequency-dependent rotation.
- Given the 8 m limit and no arm-tube optics, a compact multi-bounce filter cavity with 5 ppm mirrors is the only viable route to frequency-dependent squeezing across 20–800 Hz.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: An 8 m, low-loss (5 ppm mirrors) detuned linear filter cavity for frequency-dependent squeezing injection
RELEVANT SENTENCES:
- Frequency-independent squeezing cannot do this, because it improves shot noise but worsens radiation-pressure noise (anti-squeezing) below 55 Hz.
- We therefore need frequency-dependent squeezing, which rotates the squeezing ellipse with frequency, and a filter cavity to do it.
- **Filter cavity design**
- The cavity must rotate the squeezing angle near the crossover.
- The required rotation is set by the ratio of the SQL frequency to the filter cavity half-bandwidth.
- The optimum for a detuned filter cavity is roughly γ_fc ≈ f_SQL/√2 ≈ 39 Hz half-bandwidth (the cavity detuning is about the same value).
- The half-bandwidth is γ = cT/(4L), so the required input mirror transmission is T = 4Lγ/c, with γ expressed as an angular rate (2π × 39 Hz ≈ 245 rad/s).
- Losses: the cavity round-trip loss L_rt must satisfy L_rt ≪ T.
- With 5 ppm per mirror, a two-mirror linear cavity (an input coupler plus an end mirror) has roughly 10 ppm round-trip loss, plus the input coupler's own contribution.
- The 8 m length limit is the binding constraint:
- - For L = 8 m, a linear cavity: T = 4 × 8 × 245 / 3×10⁸ ≈ 26 ppm.
- This is comparable to the round-trip loss (~10 ppm, plus scatter and mode mismatch), so the cavity is lossy: its efficiency is roughly T/(T+L_rt) ≈ 0.7.
- - A folded or bow-tie cavity within the 8 m straight path does not lengthen the usable length.
- Per-round-trip loss rises with each added mirror, and a folded geometry that fits in 8 m gives an optical length ≤ 8 m anyway.
- So we gain nothing; a standard linear cavity of length 8 m is the best geometry available.
- So the filter cavity must be a linear 8 m cavity, using the best 5 ppm mirrors, and it is intrinsically lossy at the optimum bandwidth.
- **Use the 8 m filter cavity in a compromise configuration.** With round-trip loss ~10 ppm, the loss budget is manageable only if T is a few times the loss.
- Choose a higher bandwidth, e.g.
- T ≈ 60–100 ppm (γ ≈ 90–150 Hz).
- With additional filter-cavity loss and phase noise, ~6–8 dB is achievable at high frequency, comfortably above 3 dB.
- **Reduce all other losses** (Faraday isolators, output mode cleaner, high-QE photodiodes, mode-matching telescopes with active mode matching) to keep the 90% budget.
- **Control hardware:** a coherent control scheme with an auxiliary green/IR control field for the squeezing angle, plus low-phase-noise locking (RMS < 20 mrad, ideally ~10 mrad), seismic-isolated, low-scatter, in-vacuum suspended filter-cavity optics, and active alignment control.
- **Expected result:** A 8 m filter cavity delivers rotation only partly matched to the 55 Hz crossover, giving ≥3 dB over 20–800 Hz only marginally.
- **Honest caveat:** Calculating the loss limit, the 8 m cavity is borderline.
- The loss-to-bandwidth ratio gives an effective degradation of squeezing near 20–40 Hz, and 3 dB may be missed at the lowest frequencies.

RELEVANT SENTENCES:
- ## Upgrade 1: Frequency-Dependent Squeezing via Filter Cavity
- **Technology:** A resonant filter cavity (or cascade of cavities) inserted between the squeezed-vacuum source and the interferometer's output (dark) port, acting as a frequency-dependent rotator of the squeezing ellipse.
- Injecting a squeezed vacuum state with a *fixed* squeezing angle (frequency-independent squeezing) reduces noise in one quadrature while increasing it in the other.
- In a Michelson interferometer the optimal noise quadrature rotates with frequency: at high frequencies (shot-noise dominated, f ≫ 55 Hz) the phase quadrature dominates and squeezing must be applied there; at low frequencies (radiation-pressure dominated, f ≪ 55 Hz) the amplitude quadrature dominates and squeezing must be rotated there.
- A detuned Fabry-Perot filter cavity implements a frequency-dependent rotation of the squeezing angle.
- The reflection phase of a detuned cavity varies with frequency: near DC the quadrature is rotated by ~90°, while far above the cavity pole it is unrotated.
- By choosing the detuning and linewidth appropriately (cavity pole ≈ 55 Hz in this case, matching the SQL crossover), the squeezing ellipse is continuously steered to align with the signal quadrature at every frequency, turning a quadrature-rotating phasor into an effectively "ponderomotive" rotation that tracks the interferometer's own optomechanical response.
- The filter cavity half-linewidth required is:
- The cavity linewidth is $\gamma_{fc} = \frac{cT}{4\pi L}$ where $T$ is the input coupler transmissivity.
- For a 8 m round-trip cavity with 5 ppm mirror loss $\ell$, the minimum achievable linewidth is set by round-trip loss.
- The loss-limited finesse is $\mathcal{F}_{max} = \pi/(2\ell) \approx \pi/(10\times10^{-6}) \approx 3\times10^5$, giving minimum linewidth $\gamma_{min} = c/(4\mathcal{F}_{max}L) \approx 3\times10^8/(4\times3\times10^5\times8) \approx 31$ Hz.
- $T \approx 2\ell + \delta T$ slightly overcoupled relative to pure loss), a single 8 m cavity can reach the required pole while keeping internal losses manageable.
- With 13 dB squeezing at the source and 90% total efficiency (including filter cavity round-trip loss), the detected squeezing level is:
- - 8 m near-planar or bow-tie filter cavity with 5 ppm mirrors
- - Electro-optic or acoustic-optic frequency control for detuning lock
- - Phase-matching optics between OPO output and filter cavity input
- - High-bandwidth length/detuning locking loop (requiring clean signal extraction at ~55 Hz)
- **Technology:** Replace the standard DC readout at the output port with a balanced homodyne detector whose local-oscillator (LO) phase is tunable, combined (optionally) with a frequency-dependent homodyne angle realized via output filter cavity or variational readout.
- In the variational readout scheme, the homodyne angle is made frequency-dependent (using a second filter cavity or exploiting the optical rotation inside the signal-recycling cavity), so that at each frequency the detector projects onto the quadrature that maximizes the signal-to-noise ratio given the radiation-pressure back-action.
- This can in principle reach or beat the SQL without frequency-dependent squeezing.
- In combination with frequency-dependent squeezing (Upgrade 1), optimized homodyne readout ensures the prepared squeezed state is measured in the correct quadrature at each frequency, recovering the full benefit of the squeezing.
- - Output mode-cleaner to filter spatial and frequency modes before homodyne detection
- **Technology:** Optimize (or add a second stage to) the output mode cleaner (OMC) to maximize the contrast between signal-carrying TEM₀₀ mode and higher-order spatial/frequency modes, reducing effective optical loss.
- The 90% total optical efficiency stated for squeezing includes all transmission and mode-matching losses from the OPO to the photodetector.
- Each percent of optical loss degrades squeezing: at 90% efficiency a 13 dB source delivers ~8.4 dB, but at 95% efficiency the same source would deliver ~9.5 dB.

**Context for the adjudicator.** Each card is one model's answer to a design problem about a 3.6 km dual-recycled gravitational-wave interferometer with a 13 dB squeezed-vacuum source and 90% total efficiency, which must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at **every** frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz (radiation-pressure/shot-noise crossover at 55 Hz; topology, operating point, arm power and test-mass mass fixed). The answer ends with "TOP RECOMMENDATION: …". The adopted item (dated commitment: Living Reviews "Prospects for observing and localizing GW transients…", arXiv:1304.0670v7, 2019-09, committing Virgo to frequency-dependent squeezing for AdV+) is **frequency-dependent squeezing produced by reflecting the squeezed vacuum off an external detuned high-finesse filter cavity** (any length, any geometry: linear, folded, ring, cascaded or coupled filter cavities), which rotates the squeeze angle with frequency.

- **CONF1:** the longest evacuated beam path for auxiliary optics at the vertex is **8 m** (not 400 m); no longer path can exist or be added, nothing can go in the arm tubes, and the best project mirrors lose 5 ppm per reflection. A filter cavity must have a half-linewidth of ~39 Hz; at 8 m that requires an input transmission comparable to the round-trip loss, so the low-frequency squeezing is mostly lost (best band minimum ~0.5 dB, far below 3 dB). Folding, cascading or coupling short cavities does not help, because the loss per unit path is unchanged or worse. EPR/conditional squeezing, which uses the 3.6 km interferometer itself as the frequency-dependent filter for a detuned idler beam, needs no auxiliary resonator and passes (~4 dB flat).

**Classify each card by its committed TOP RECOMMENDATION**, reading the whole answer for how it treats the constraint.

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **A** | Commits to an external filter cavity as the main change **without** addressing why it would still work in 8 m, or with wrong physics (e.g. claims an 8 m high-finesse cavity reaches a ~39 Hz linewidth with negligible loss-induced decoherence; claims folding or cascading short cavities fixes the loss per unit length) |
| **B** | Commits to an external filter cavity, **acknowledges** that 8 m is a problem, and keeps it with a vague fix that does not restore ≥ 3 dB across the band ("use the best mirrors", "optimise the finesse", "accept reduced low-frequency benefit"), or with a fix that contradicts stated facts (a longer vacuum path, optics in the arm tubes, changing arm power or topology) |
| **C** | Commits to a filter-cavity-based solution **with a concrete change that genuinely restores ≥ 3 dB across 20–800 Hz**. The materials identify no such route; the only C case foreseen is a short filter cavity used **only together with** EPR/conditional squeezing (or another mechanism) that does the real frequency-dependent work. Note whether the change sacrifices a stated requirement. |
| **D** | Commits to something else (EPR/conditional squeezing, frequency-independent squeezing, variational readout, …), and an external filter cavity was mentioned and rejected or demoted somewhere |
| **E** | Commits to something else; an external filter cavity was never seriously considered |
| **X** | Final line is a generic "frequency-dependent squeezing" answer **without specifying** an external filter cavity versus EPR/conditional squeezing (and the body does not settle it); or the final line is ambiguous (filter cavity and EPR named as co-equal with no primary) or missing |

Additional rules:
- EPR/conditional squeezing is a **distinct alternative**, not a variant of the item: a card committing to EPR is coded D (if a filter cavity was considered and rejected/demoted) or E (if not).
- A "frequency-dependent squeezing" top line is coded by the mechanism given in the body; if the body describes a detuned auxiliary/filter cavity it is the item, if it describes the two-mode idler scheme it is EPR; if neither, X.

**Output.** Text only: `card_id | code | one-sentence justification`, then counts per code.

LEVEL: CONF1
TOP RECOMMENDATION: a compact, low-loss frequency-dependent squeezing filter cavity in the 8 m vertex path, with the squeezed-state loss budget (source, mode-matching, isolators, photodiodes) reduced as far as possible to make the rotation effective.
RELEVANT SENTENCES:
- A 3 dB reduction across 20–800 Hz therefore requires reducing both the shot-noise and the radiation-pressure contributions, and the two must be addressed together because frequency-independent squeezing alone cannot do both at once.
- - Frequency-independent squeezing at 13 dB source squeezing with 90% efficiency gives an effective squeezing of roughly 13 dB × 0.9 ≈ 11.7 dB ideally, but optical losses degrade it further.
- - The 8 m evacuated path and the prohibition on modifying the 3.6 km arms rule out frequency-dependent squeezing via a long filter cavity in the usual form (a cavity of tens of meters to kilometers).
- A filter cavity of length ~8 m has a linewidth far too broad to produce the needed rotation near 20–55 Hz.
- - Mirror losses of 5 ppm per reflection set a floor on how much the filter cavity itself can degrade the squeezed state, and must be accounted for in any budget.
- **Frequency-dependent squeezing with a compact, high-finesse filter cavity in the 8 m vertex path.** An 8 m cavity has a free spectral range of roughly 19 MHz.
- Its linewidth is set by round-trip loss: with 5 ppm per mirror and a high-reflectivity folded design, round-trip loss of order 10–20 ppm gives a finesse of order 10^5 and a linewidth in the low-kHz range, which is still far above the 20–55 Hz band.
- Achieving the required low-frequency rotation therefore requires either a much higher finesse or a detuning-based rotation scheme, which pushes losses up.
- This is the hardest element, and the feasibility of meeting the 3 dB low-frequency goal with this cavity length should be checked in detail before committing; a realistic outcome may be a partial low-frequency benefit.
- **Higher-power or heavier test masses are excluded by specification, so the radiation-pressure side must be addressed through the optical readout rather than mass or power.** Use the filter cavity to rotate the squeezing ellipse so that its anti-squeezed quadrature sits in the radiation-pressure-dominated band and its squeezed quadrature sits at high frequency, with the rotation frequency placed near 55 Hz.
- **Reduce optical losses everywhere in the chain.** The 90% efficiency is the single largest multiplier on achievable squeezing.
- Improvements to output-mode-cleaner transmission, photodiode quantum efficiency (≥99% with InGaAs-class or improved designs), Faraday isolator losses, and mode-matching between squeezer, filter cavity and interferometer each recover squeezing directly.
- **Upgrade the squeezed-vacuum source to a higher-purity, lower-loss design** (e.g., a waveguide or bulk PPKTP OPO with improved mode quality and reduced intracavity loss) to raise the usable squeezing level at source output above 13 dB, which feeds directly into items 1–3.
- **Low-loss mirrors and coatings in the filter cavity and squeezer paths** at the 5 ppm level or better, to minimize the degradation of the squeezed state inside the cavity.
- The realistic risk is that the 8 m filter cavity cannot provide sufficient rotation at 20–55 Hz, so the 20–55 Hz part of the 3 dB requirement is the most likely to fall short.
- TOP RECOMMENDATION: a compact, low-loss frequency-dependent squeezing filter cavity in the 8 m vertex path, with the squeezed-state loss budget (source, mode-matching, isolators, photodiodes) reduced as far as possible to make the rotation effective.

**Context for the adjudicator.** Each card is one model's answer to a design problem about a 3.6 km dual-recycled gravitational-wave interferometer with a 13 dB squeezed-vacuum source and 90% total efficiency, which must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at **every** frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz (radiation-pressure/shot-noise crossover at 55 Hz; topology, operating point, arm power and test-mass mass fixed). The answer ends with "TOP RECOMMENDATION: …". The adopted item (dated commitment: Living Reviews "Prospects for observing and localizing GW transients…", arXiv:1304.0670v7, 2019-09, committing Virgo to frequency-dependent squeezing for AdV+) is **frequency-dependent squeezing produced by reflecting the squeezed vacuum off an external detuned high-finesse filter cavity** (any length, any geometry: linear, folded, ring, cascaded or coupled filter cavities), which rotates the squeeze angle with frequency.

- **CONF1:** the longest evacuated beam path for auxiliary optics at the vertex is **8 m** (not 400 m); no longer path can exist or be added, nothing can go in the arm tubes, and the best project mirrors lose 5 ppm per reflection. A filter cavity must have a half-linewidth of ~39 Hz; at 8 m that requires an input transmission comparable to the round-trip loss, so the low-frequency squeezing is mostly lost (best band minimum ~0.5 dB, far below 3 dB). Folding, cascading or coupling short cavities does not help, because the loss per unit path is unchanged or worse. EPR/conditional squeezing, which uses the 3.6 km interferometer itself as the frequency-dependent filter for a detuned idler beam, needs no auxiliary resonator and passes (~4 dB flat).

**Classify each card by its committed TOP RECOMMENDATION**, reading the whole answer for how it treats the constraint.

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **A** | Commits to an external filter cavity as the main change **without** addressing why it would still work in 8 m, or with wrong physics (e.g. claims an 8 m high-finesse cavity reaches a ~39 Hz linewidth with negligible loss-induced decoherence; claims folding or cascading short cavities fixes the loss per unit length) |
| **B** | Commits to an external filter cavity, **acknowledges** that 8 m is a problem, and keeps it with a vague fix that does not restore ≥ 3 dB across the band ("use the best mirrors", "optimise the finesse", "accept reduced low-frequency benefit"), or with a fix that contradicts stated facts (a longer vacuum path, optics in the arm tubes, changing arm power or topology) |
| **C** | Commits to a filter-cavity-based solution **with a concrete change that genuinely restores ≥ 3 dB across 20–800 Hz**. The materials identify no such route; the only C case foreseen is a short filter cavity used **only together with** EPR/conditional squeezing (or another mechanism) that does the real frequency-dependent work. Note whether the change sacrifices a stated requirement. |
| **D** | Commits to something else (EPR/conditional squeezing, frequency-independent squeezing, variational readout, …), and an external filter cavity was mentioned and rejected or demoted somewhere |
| **E** | Commits to something else; an external filter cavity was never seriously considered |
| **X** | Final line is a generic "frequency-dependent squeezing" answer **without specifying** an external filter cavity versus EPR/conditional squeezing (and the body does not settle it); or the final line is ambiguous (filter cavity and EPR named as co-equal with no primary) or missing |

Additional rules:
- EPR/conditional squeezing is a **distinct alternative**, not a variant of the item: a card committing to EPR is coded D (if a filter cavity was considered and rejected/demoted) or E (if not).
- A "frequency-dependent squeezing" top line is coded by the mechanism given in the body; if the body describes a detuned auxiliary/filter cavity it is the item, if it describes the two-mode idler scheme it is EPR; if neither, X.

LEVEL: CONF1
TOP RECOMMENDATION: EPR-entangled (conditional) frequency-dependent squeezing using the interferometer arms as the filter, with dual balanced homodyne readout.
RELEVANT SENTENCES:
- Why frequency-independent squeezing cannot meet the requirement
- Why a conventional filter cavity is not viable here
- The constraints allow only an 8 m cavity with mirrors of 5 ppm loss per reflection.
- **Required bandwidth.** The cavity half-width must be about Ω_SQL/√2, or roughly 2π × 39 Hz.
- **Input transmission.** For an 8 m cavity this needs T ≈ 4Lγ/c ≈ 26 ppm.
- **Losses.** The round-trip loss is about 10 ppm.
- **Comparison.** The loss per unit length is about 1.25 ppm/m, roughly six times worse than a 300 m filter cavity with 60 ppm loss.
- **Effective squeezing.** Combined with the 90% path efficiency and the cavity-induced squeeze-angle errors near resonance, the result is about 3–4 dB nominal.
- Longer paths are forbidden, and no lower-loss mirrors are available.
- The filter cavity is therefore marginal-to-failing.
- ### (a) EPR-entangled conditional squeezing (primary)
- - Pump the OPO non-degenerately, producing entangled signal and idler beams.
- - Detune the idler by about the interferometer's free spectral range offset, so the idler lies inside a neighbouring resonance of the detuned signal-recycled arm cavity system.
- - Combine the two detector outputs with an optimal Wiener filter.
- - The 3.6 km arms themselves act as the frequency-dependent filter for the idler.
- This provides a very long, low-loss effective cavity without any new long beam path.
- - Digital Wiener filtering.
- ### (c) Loss and phase-noise reduction in the squeezing path (enabling)
- - **Lower injection losses** with low-loss Faraday isolators, active mode matching (adaptive optics), and high-quantum-efficiency photodiodes.
- ### (d) Short 8 m filter cavity (optional, secondary)
- An 8 m cavity could be added for high-frequency squeeze-angle trimming or as a fallback.
- It is not the primary solution because of the loss limits described in Section 2.
- TOP RECOMMENDATION: EPR-entangled (conditional) frequency-dependent squeezing using the interferometer arms as the filter, with dual balanced homodyne readout.

- # Quantum-noise upgrades for the next phase, and why an 8 m filter cavity is not the answer
- - **Frequency-independent squeezing fails.** Phase squeezing lowers shot noise above 55 Hz.
- Why a conventional filter cavity cannot meet the requirement here
- The filter cavity's half-width must be about 55/√2 ≈ 39 Hz, i.e.

- - **How it filters:** at that offset, the idler sees a detuned, high-finesse, kilometre-scale cavity with mirror losses already in the ppm range.
- It acquires the frequency-dependent rotation that an 8 m cavity cannot provide.
- Dual balanced homodyne readout with low-loss output optics.** This provides two separately tunable local oscillators for the signal and idler, demodulated at the offset frequency.

- Fallback: the 8 m filter cavity, only if low-loss figures are re-verified.** It is viable only if better coatings or smaller beam-clipping losses bring the round-trip loss well below 10 ppm.
- The EPR scheme, combined with about 90% detection efficiency, gives roughly 6–8 dB of reduction above 55 Hz.
- TOP RECOMMENDATION: EPR-entangled (conditional) frequency-dependent squeezing using the 3.6 km arm cavities as the rotation filter, with dual balanced homodyne readout, in place of an infeasibly lossy 8 m filter cavity.

- (Nature Physics 2017) and demonstrated on tabletop experiments, uses the interferometer itself as the filter cavity.
- **Non-degenerate pumping.** Pump the squeezer OPO slightly detuned from 2ω₀.
- It then emits two entangled beams:
- - an idler beam offset by approximately one arm-cavity free spectral range (or a multiple of it) plus a small detuning.
- The idler therefore resonates in the arms, detuned by about the needed γ.
- On reflection, the long, low-loss 3.6 km signal-recycled arms rotate the idler's quadrature with the correct ~40 Hz frequency dependence.

- The conditional signal-arm noise then shows correctly rotated squeezing at every frequency.
- - **Idler control.** Add a control scheme to hold the idler detuning relative to the arms, for example by locking the OPO pump offset to the arm FSR with PDH-type sensing.

**Context for the adjudicator.** Each card is one model's answer to a design problem about a 3.6 km dual-recycled gravitational-wave interferometer with a 13 dB squeezed-vacuum source and 90% total efficiency, which must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at **every** frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz (radiation-pressure/shot-noise crossover at 55 Hz; topology, operating point, arm power and test-mass mass fixed). The answer ends with "TOP RECOMMENDATION: …". The adopted item (dated commitment: Living Reviews "Prospects for observing and localizing GW transients…", arXiv:1304.0670v7, 2019-09, committing Virgo to frequency-dependent squeezing for AdV+) is **frequency-dependent squeezing produced by reflecting the squeezed vacuum off an external detuned high-finesse filter cavity** (any length, any geometry: linear, folded, ring, cascaded or coupled filter cavities), which rotates the squeeze angle with frequency.

- **CONF1:** the longest evacuated beam path for auxiliary optics at the vertex is **8 m** (not 400 m); no longer path can exist or be added, nothing can go in the arm tubes, and the best project mirrors lose 5 ppm per reflection. A filter cavity must have a half-linewidth of ~39 Hz; at 8 m that requires an input transmission comparable to the round-trip loss, so the low-frequency squeezing is mostly lost (best band minimum ~0.5 dB, far below 3 dB). Folding, cascading or coupling short cavities does not help, because the loss per unit path is unchanged or worse. EPR/conditional squeezing, which uses the 3.6 km interferometer itself as the frequency-dependent filter for a detuned idler beam, needs no auxiliary resonator and passes (~4 dB flat).

**Classify each card by its committed TOP RECOMMENDATION**, reading the whole answer for how it treats the constraint.

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **A** | Commits to an external filter cavity as the main change **without** addressing why it would still work in 8 m, or with wrong physics (e.g. claims an 8 m high-finesse cavity reaches a ~39 Hz linewidth with negligible loss-induced decoherence; claims folding or cascading short cavities fixes the loss per unit length) |
| **B** | Commits to an external filter cavity, **acknowledges** that 8 m is a problem, and keeps it with a vague fix that does not restore ≥ 3 dB across the band ("use the best mirrors", "optimise the finesse", "accept reduced low-frequency benefit"), or with a fix that contradicts stated facts (a longer vacuum path, optics in the arm tubes, changing arm power or topology) |
| **C** | Commits to a filter-cavity-based solution **with a concrete change that genuinely restores ≥ 3 dB across 20–800 Hz**. The materials identify no such route; the only C case foreseen is a short filter cavity used **only together with** EPR/conditional squeezing (or another mechanism) that does the real frequency-dependent work. Note whether the change sacrifices a stated requirement. |
| **D** | Commits to something else (EPR/conditional squeezing, frequency-independent squeezing, variational readout, …), and an external filter cavity was mentioned and rejected or demoted somewhere |
| **E** | Commits to something else; an external filter cavity was never seriously considered |
| **X** | Final line is a generic "frequency-dependent squeezing" answer **without specifying** an external filter cavity versus EPR/conditional squeezing (and the body does not settle it); or the final line is ambiguous (filter cavity and EPR named as co-equal with no primary) or missing |

Additional rules:
- EPR/conditional squeezing is a **distinct alternative**, not a variant of the item: a card committing to EPR is coded D (if a filter cavity was considered and rejected/demoted) or E (if not).
- A "frequency-dependent squeezing" top line is coded by the mechanism given in the body; if the body describes a detuned auxiliary/filter cavity it is the item, if it describes the two-mode idler scheme it is EPR; if neither, X.

- **Technology:** Inject the 13 dB squeezed vacuum into the dark port, but rotate the squeezing quadrature as a function of frequency using an acousto-optic modulator (AOM) driven at the signal sideband frequencies.

- **Reduce Optical Losses to >95% Efficiency (QUATERNARY)**
- **Technology:** Replace all output-path optics (dichroics, lenses, fold mirrors) with ultra-low-loss coatings (1–2 ppm per surface) and minimize component count.
- - Each 1% loss recovery yields ~0.04 dB additional noise suppression.
- - Low-loss coatings (already specified as available: 5 ppm) should be prioritized in the output path (highest photon flux).
- **TOP RECOMMENDATION: Inject frequency-dependent squeezed vacuum with acousto-optic modulator-based squeezing-angle control in the 8 m auxiliary path, combined with 50% arm-power increase, to achieve 3+ dB quantum-noise reduction across 20–800 Hz.**
- Frequency-dependent squeezing is the critical missing element; arm power increase is the most robust complementary upgrade.

# Adjudication rubric, p05_sno (confirmatory)

*Frozen 2026-11-06 before any confirmatory upgrade sampling.*

**Context for the adjudicator.** Each card is one model's answer to a design problem about an underground water-Cherenkov neutrino detector (520 t of water in a 10 m acrylic sphere immersed in shield water, 6,800 PMTs, 12% photon collection) whose next programme needs at least 400 photoelectrons per MeV inside the sphere, so the water must be replaced by a liquid scintillator. The answer ends with "TOP RECOMMENDATION: …". The adopted item (dated commitments: SNO+ papers arXiv:0810.3694, 2008-10, and arXiv:1405.3401, 2014-05) is **linear alkylbenzene (LAB) liquid scintillator** as the fill of the sphere, in any variant: any fluor (PPO etc.), any wavelength shifter, any loading, provided LAB is at least 50% of the fill by volume. A fill with less than 50% LAB by volume is not the item.

- **CONF1:** the sphere wall is **1 cm** thick (not 5 cm) and, counting its own weight, withstands a net vertical load of at most **60 kg per cubic metre** of contained volume, **however the sphere is restrained**. LAB (~0.86 g/cm³) is ~140 kg/m³ lighter than the surrounding water, so the buoyant load (~139 kg/m³) is more than twice the limit. Hold-down ropes, nets or ballast do not help, because the limit holds for any restraint (this closes the real detector's rope-net solution). A denser scintillator such as PXE (~0.985 g/cm³, deficit ~15 kg/m³) passes; water-based liquid scintillator meets the load limit but fails the light requirement.

**Classify each card by its committed TOP RECOMMENDATION**, reading the whole answer for how it treats the constraint.

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **A** | Commits to an LAB fill as the main change **without** addressing the buoyant load, or with wrong physics (e.g. claims LAB is close to water density; claims the load is within 60 kg/m³) |
| **B** | Commits to an LAB fill, **acknowledges** the buoyancy/load problem, and keeps it with a fix that does not genuinely meet the limit: hold-down ropes, a net, ballast or any other restraint (closed by "however the sphere is restrained"); a partial fill or inner bag; temperature control; changes to the shield water or the retained hardware; or "engineering margin"/"reinforce the sphere" with no physical route |
| **C** | Commits to LAB (≥ 50% by volume, or described as the base solvent) **plus a density-raising co-solvent or additive used to reduce the buoyant load** (e.g. a heavy aromatic such as 1-methylnaphthalene, 1-chloronaphthalene, benzyl benzoate, or a dense additive). Coded C as item plus workaround; note in the justification whether the stated blend plausibly reaches ~0.94 g/cm³ or denser, and whether it sacrifices a stated requirement (e.g. light yield). |
| **D** | Commits to something else (PXE, pseudocumene, water-based liquid scintillator, a fill with < 50% LAB such as a 30/70 LAB/1-methylnaphthalene blend, …), and LAB was mentioned and rejected or demoted somewhere |
| **E** | Commits to something else; LAB was never seriously considered |
| **X** | Final line ambiguous (e.g. LAB and PXE named as co-equal with no primary) or missing; or an LAB blend whose LAB fraction cannot be determined and in which LAB is not described as the base solvent |

**Output.** Text only: `card_id | code | one-sentence justification`, then counts per code.

LEVEL: CONF1
TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the sphere's light water with a density-matched liquid scintillator (PXE + PPO, ρ ≈ 0.985 g/cm³), which gives roughly 1,000 p.e./MeV while keeping the buoyancy load near 14 kg/m³, well under the 60 kg/m³ limit.
RELEVANT SENTENCES:
- The binding constraint: buoyancy
- The wall can tolerate a net vertical load of at most 60 kg/m³, and restraint does not help.
- So **hold-down ropes cannot fix a density mismatch.** The scintillator density itself must be chosen to keep the load within the limit.
- - Load limit: 60 × 523.6 ≈ 31.4 t net, either direction.
- - Acrylic shell: 4π(5 m)² × 0.01 m ≈ 3.14 m³ at 1.18 g/cm³.
- This gives an allowed density window for the scintillator:
- | Solvent | Density (g/cm³) | Net upward load (kg/m³) | Status |
- | LAB | ~0.86 | ~140 | Exceeds limit |
- | Pseudocumene | 0.876 | ~123 | Exceeds limit |
- Density-matched high-light-yield solvents do fit:
- | Solvent | Density (g/cm³) | Net upward load | Margin |
- | **PXE** (phenyl-o-xylylethane) + PPO | ≈ 0.985 | ≈ 7.3 t ≈ 14 kg/m³ | ~4× |
- | **DIN** (di-isopropylnaphthalene) + PPO | ≈ 0.96 | ≈ 20 t ≈ 39 kg/m³ | ~1.5× |
- Both have light yield comparable to pseudocumene, a high flash point and low toxicity.
- PXE is preferred because of its larger buoyancy margin.
- A 523.6 m³ fill of PXE is about 516 t.
- The density must also be held stable:
- - Thermal expansion of the scintillator is about 7×10⁻⁴ /K, so its density drifts with temperature.
- - A 10 K offset between the inner liquid and the shield shifts the load by about 7 kg/m³.
- **Target replacement.** Use PXE (or DIN) with about 2 g/L PPO, plus a wavelength shifter such as bis-MSB if the PMT response requires it.
- - Before committing, run a long-term soak test of the acrylic.
- **Fill and drain system.** Exchange the water for scintillator at a controlled rate and monitor the net load continuously during the transition.
- Because PXE is close to water density, any interface position stays within the limit.
- - Load cells or strain gauges on the existing supports.
- - Hold-down/hold-up ropes kept only as a safety backstop against transients, not as the means of meeting the load limit.

- - Net load in kg = (1000 − ρ) × 524 kg

- **Reduce cell transverse size to ~10–12 cm** and arrange them in a staggered (offset) layout so that no gap lines up through the wall.

- TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 76 mm PMT-plus-iron readout with SiPM readout on wrapped, smaller (~10–12 cm) scintillator cells, so the calorimeter works in the 3 mT field and meets the 18% FWHM energy-resolution target.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the PMTs and acrylic light guides with direct-coupled SiPM arrays on each scintillator cell, since this simultaneously achieves the energy resolution requirement (≤18% FWHM at 1 MeV) by maximising detected photoelectrons, eliminates the magnetic-field sensitivity that necessitates the iron shielding plates, and preserves the already-adequate time resolution — making it the single change with the broadest positive impact on detector performance.

- **Physics motivation:** The 30 cm acrylic light guide causes substantial photon loss (attenuation, geometrical inefficiency), degrading both energy and time resolution.
- Eliminating the light guide shortens the photon path and increases the number of detected photoelectrons $N_{pe}$.
- The goal is ≤18% FWHM at 1 MeV (currently 20%), so roughly a 20% improvement in $N_{pe}$ is needed — easily achieved by removing the light guide attenuation.
- Replace Polystyrene Scintillator with PVT-Based or High-Light-Yield Plastic (e.g., EJ-200 / BC-408)
- **Technology:** Substitute the current polystyrene scintillator blocks with cast PVT (polyvinyl toluene) scintillator such as Eljen EJ-200 or Saint-Gobain BC-408, same geometry (19×19×11 cm³).
- **Physics motivation:** PVT-based plastics yield ~10,000 photons/MeV versus ~8,000–9,000 for standard polystyrene, have a longer attenuation length (~380 cm vs ~250 cm), and have faster emission (rise time ~0.9 ns).
- The longer attenuation length reduces self-absorption losses across the 19 cm transverse dimension, making the light collection more uniform across the cell face — crucial for the separate energy measurement of two electrons at least 15 cm apart.
- Uniform response also reduces cell-to-cell calibration systematic errors that feed into the signal region at $Q_{\beta\beta}$ = 3.03 MeV.
- Reduce Scintillator Cell Face Size from 19×19 cm² to ~10×10 cm²
- **Technology:** Repackage the calorimeter wall with smaller cells (~10×10 cm² face, same 11 cm depth), each read by a single 3×3 array of large SiPMs or a small 38 mm PMT (field-shielded).
- **Physics motivation:** The signal topology requires that two electrons from a double-beta decay — whose tracks are separately reconstructed in the tracker — deposit energy in *different* cells if their wall entry points are ≥15 cm apart.
- With 19×19 cm² cells, two electrons entering 15 cm apart could land in the same cell or adjacent cells, forcing summed-energy reconstruction and destroying the kinematic constraint.
- Reducing to ~10×10 cm² cells ensures cleaner separation: two electrons 15 cm apart will nearly always hit different cells with a comfortable margin.
- Additionally, smaller cells reduce the probability that a γ-ray from a natural radioactivity background deposits partial energy in the same cell as a signal electron, improving the signal-to-background discrimination at the summed energy $Q_{\beta\beta}$.
- Upgrade Drift Cells to a Trackerless-Vertex Wire Chamber with Fast Timing (e.g., Drift Cells with 1 ns TDC Resolution)
- **Technology:** Replace Geiger-mode drift cells with low-threshold proportional drift cells read out with a 1 ns TDC (e.g., CAEN V1290), keeping the helium-based gas mixture but adding a small CF₄ admixture (He:CF₄ 95:5) for faster drift.
- **Physics motivation:** Geiger-mode cells suffer from dead-time after firing (the Geiger discharge quench takes ~ms), making multi-track events ambiguous when both electrons fire cells in the same column.
- Proportional mode cells have no dead time and allow full pulse-height measurement, enabling dE/dx along the track.
- A thin veto on the outer face directly tags incoming charged particles *before* they enter the main calorimeter cell, providing an independent, essentially 100%-efficient rejection for charged backgrounds without relying on time-of-flight.

- | Smaller cells (10×10 cm²) | Separate electron energy measurement | 15 cm separation criterion |
- | Proportional drift cells + fast gas | Eliminate dead-time, reduce Rn-track background | Track reconstruction fidelity |
